Everyone's gatekeeping their YC Startup School group chats. You can join mine right now, no strings attached... Y Combinator 's Startup School is bringing together some incredibly talented, high-signal young people from around the world in SF later this month. And yet it remains so hard to leverage that network; there's no searchable directory you get access to, and no official forum in which you can connect with other attendees. There are unofficial groups, but their entire premise is built on exclusivity - someone needs to be convinced that you're worth enough to be let in, regardless of if you've been accepted to the actual event! At the same time, I noticed that so many accomplished individuals - builders, researchers, founders, and otherwise - didn't apply or are still waiting to hear back, and for that reason it would be valuable to build a community that caters to a broader range of high-achievers in the long term. I want to fix these gaps. I've been building inclusive communities online since middle school, when I once made a Google Classroom with hundreds of classmates and posted about local news, events, important information, etc. It was literally called "As Much Of Town As Possible". I didn't want to leave anyone behind. And so, I've created a Discord server that anyone can join. My vision is that it'll be active long after Startup School as folks share events, ideas, and opportunities. We've already got biotech founders, VCs, and even the youngest ever YC hackathon winner. If you *are* attending Startup School, you can self-verify to automatically access the relevant channels and (soon) a directory of attendees! You don't need to hope that someone will read your comment. You don't need to wait for someone to accept your request. You can just join. Why wait? Find my comment below for the link! ...more

All my friends are too busy, so I'm building AI agents to play Minecraft with me instead. I'm at the Y Combinator office right now for HUD 's RSI and RL Environments hackathon - my ninth YC hackathon so far - and I decided to build something fun that'd also teach me more about these technologies. A few years ago, I saw a viral video about AI-powered Minecraft bots that "simulated civilization." They formed "cultures" and waged "wars." This piqued my curiosity immediately, and hasn't left my mind since. I thought it would be incredible to simulate factions of intelligent agents roaming an open world, gathering resources, dividing tasks, and achieving goals together. To my dismay, the project was closed-source, and no further updates have come out of it since that original demo. By 2026 standards, the technology available at the time that project was made is already aging. Multimodal LLMs, tool calling, structured output, reasoning, and the exponential improvement of the models overall make this project even more feasible than before - indeed, I think I can do better than the original if I continue beyond this hackathon! So far, the agents are capable of: - Navigating, fighting, gathering resources, and other basic abilities - Long and short-term planning and goals - Communicating with each other (or humans) to share info or divide tasks - Social intelligence - remembering good/bad interactions, holding grudges, etc. - "Imagining" and building complex structures Anyways, I'm posting this before the hackathon is even over for two reasons: 1. There's a Most Viral track 😅 2. I'd love to have humans play alongside my agents! If you'd like to play with the agents, comment or DM and I'll share access to a test server very shortly. ...more

You can move your chats between Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor now. Here’s how. Recently, I wanted to resume working on a project I had started a few months ago in Cursor. Having gotten more accustomed to Claude Code, I wanted to use Claude Code instead of Cursor moving forward. However, my Cursor chats held context that I couldn’t port into Claude, making for a rough handoff. The great thing about writing software in 2026 is there's no reason to wait for solutions to your problems. I vibe coded an MVP by lunchtime on a random Sunday when I felt like it. My initial challenge of porting Cursor chats to Claude Code was solved. But then I got ambitious: I wanted to implement the opposite migration path, as well as add support for other coding agents. This required some creativity - telling Claude to “add Codex support, make no mistakes” would be futile, because it had no way to verify its work without me manually attempting migrations and visually confirming everything looked correct over and over. So then I built my own end-to-end verification loop for CLI development. The end result was that Claude could add support for other agents without any intervention on my part! This became a distinct project that deserves a separate writeup. In the meantime, try out agent-migrator. You can install it with one command: uv tool install agent-migrator Then, in any project directory where you’ve used Claude Code CLI, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, or Cursor IDE, simply run: agent-migrator Pick your source and target agents, select the chats you want to migrate, and submit. The chats you started with one coding agent instantly become visible to another - a useful ability considering Claude’s rather disappointing uptime, and the fact that a different company releases the latest “most powerful” coding model every two weeks. It’s open source. Check out the repo at the link in the comments! I even included a Claude Code plugin that auto-migrates your chat when you start hitting API errors. ...more

Won another YC Hackathon, and this time I met Garry Tan ! Last Saturday I was at my fourth Y Combinator hackathon, where we were tasked with using Garry Tan's "AI brain" framework, GBrain. GBrain ingests knowledge in any format, recalling information coherently over long periods of time and large volumes of data. It's meant to act as an extension of yourself or the sum of all your organization's knowledge. For this project, my teammate Holly T. leaned into her research experience in the medical field, ultimately identifying the problem we aimed to solve: junior radiologists need a way to improve their ability to analyze scans even when senior colleagues aren't available to assess their work. We didn't just guess that this problem existed. We first spoke to Yuva Krishnapillai , a Stanford-based brain researcher and founder whose insights offered initial validation for our idea. During the event, we even managed to chat with Dr. Michał Nedoszytko MD, PhD , the cardiologist who famously won at Anthropic 's global hackathon. After we demoed what we had built by that point, we asked upfront if he would find the product useful if we completed it and he were our target user, and he said yes! Filled with confidence, we doubled down on implementing a few points of feedback he had offered, and soon enough we submitted our project. We demoed live on stage, and then eagerly waited for the judges to deliberate. As someone who's been to several YC hackathons, this one held more weight than usual since Garry himself was among the judges. Eventually, it was time for the winners to be announced. Team after team walked onstage and posed for photos - and then they called up our team, Cortex! We thought we misheard the announcer for a moment, and then rushed to the stage. Turns out we were a winner in the GBrain track! This time around I didn't win cash... but I did get to exchange contact info with Garry! And he gave us signed hats. In any case, this hackathon was the first time I explored GStack and GBrain, as well as the first time I built anything for the healthcare industry. The whole experience was very inspiring, and I'm looking forward to the next hackathon. Thanks once again to my teammate Holly and to the event organizers! P.S. I have some other exciting YC-related news to share in the coming days 👀 ...more

I've started going to hackathons every single weekend while I'm in SF. It's not about stacking up wins. Every hackathon is an opportunity to broaden your horizons, both in terms of technical experience and meeting new people. Most hackathons will encourage participants to build projects that relate to a given niche, or that utilize specific technologies. Those events are great for pushing yourself out of your comfort zone; before coming to SF, I had never built projects involving voice agents, edge inference, ChatGPT addons, Meta glasses, prediction markets, generative video, and the list goes on. Nothing was stopping me from exploring those technologies on my own, but hackathons forced me to actually become competent in them within a short time frame. Moreover, hackathons are an excellent source of inspiration as a prospective entrepreneur. I've found that attending these events keeps me ahead of the curve in terms of emerging technologies and the types of problems they can solve. Generally, I think there's a lot of overlap between good hackathon ideas and good startup ideas - the winning projects usually have identified a genuine pain point felt by real people which they've solved using innovative technology. Having to build useful, demoable products within a single day (or even just a few hours!) each weekend helps me train that entrepreneurial muscle as I explore my own ideas and come across new problems to solve. On the non-technical side, hackathons are also an excellent way to meet interesting people and push yourself out of your comfort zone. Outside of college-affiliated hackathons, I often find that I'm among the youngest in the room, but that's not a bad thing! At those events, I'm often surrounded by startup founders, senior engineers, top researchers, and serious builders who I can always learn something from. Simultaneously, I sometimes still run into people younger than myself - even high school students - who inspire me through their boldness and creativity. In the same vein, hackathons are an easy way to get noticed. Some of my best-performing posts on LinkedIn have been about hackathons I've gone to, and the projects I've built have made me much more noticeable. Of course, the people you make an impression on when you demo at these events can be highly valuable, too - consider TreeHacks , HackMIT , or the various Y Combinator hackathons I've gone to recently, for example! Anyways, I'm heading to yet another hackathon today over at UC Berkeley, and some bigger ones later this month. If you'd like to team up at a hackathon in the bay sometime, send me a message! And if a detailed breakdown about my hackathon strategies would be useful, do let me know. Pictured below: my most recent hackathon teammate Pablo Ramírez Ortiz (a startup founder from Ecuador!) and I at Beta Fund 's 'Builders of Tomorrow' hackathon last weekend. ...more

I'm incredibly grateful for the opportunity to have served as an Ambassador for the Schiffer Family Financial Literacy Program this year. Through this experience, I had the privilege of working with students at North Brunswick Township High School and Franklin High School, helping them build a stronger understanding of personal finance and the importance of financial literacy at a young age. A special thank you to the Schiffer team of ambassadors, program directors Ron Richter and Luke Greeley, PhD , and especially Anna Wingerter and Ted Olswfski who I worked closely with throughout the program. Their passion for expanding financial education made this experience both rewarding and inspiring. It was exciting to engage with students, answer their questions, and hopefully make a small impact on how they think about budgeting, saving, investing, and making informed financial decisions. Financial literacy is a life skill, and I'm proud to have contributed to an initiative that empowers the next generation with the knowledge and confidence to make smarter financial choices. Thank you to everyone involved for making this such a meaningful experience. I look forward to continue expanding the Schiffer program and to support initiatives that promote education and community impact. #FinancialLiteracy #CommunityImpact #Education #Leadership #Volunteer #SchifferFinancialLiteracy #FinancialEducation #GivingBack

It’s been a busy summer. I started it off studying abroad in Switzerland at FHNW Basel with 15 other designers, under the instruction of Mark Laughlin and with support from our wonderful program assistant, Lauren Violette . I had an incredible time and learned so much about typography, design, and how I approach creative work. I’ve spent the rest of the summer interning at Interplanetary Help Desk , a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, where I’ve worked across social media and graphic design while also helping negotiate paid marketing partnerships and sponsorships. More recently, I joined Northeastern’s Entrepreneurship Club (E-Club) as Design Director. I’m excited to work alongside such a talented team and help shape the visual identity of Northeastern’s largest business club this semester. And finally, after a lot of work, I finished and published my portfolio! Check it out: annabelledavis.xyz It’s been a full summer, and it looks like it’ll be an equally busy fall as I begin searching for co-op opportunities in the design and marketing space. If you know of a team, role, or opportunity you think I’d be a good fit for, I’d love to hear about it.

Seattle folks working on AI agents: we’re hosting a hands-on workshop on August 25 focused on building strong eval foundations. If you’re an AI engineer, ML practitioner, or technical PM trying to understand what your agent is actually doing, how to measure quality, and how to improve it across iterations, this is for you. We’ll cover how to: • Observe agent behavior step by step • Build evals that measure what matters • Score runs and track quality over time • Turn production behavior into a practical eval workflow No prior eval experience is required. Just bring a laptop. We already have an incredible group registered, including AI builders, engineers, and product leaders from companies building some of the most exciting AI products today, plus founders from across the PNW AI community. 📍 RailSpur rooftop, Seattle 📅 Tuesday, August 25 ⏰ 3 to 6 PM Plus drinks, networking, and a pretty great view of the Seattle skyline and Puget Sound. Register here: luma.com/seattle-workshop If you know someone in Seattle building agents who would get value from this, send it their way.
